tier_reason: The only figure is a bare 'faster by a factor of two on my machine' in an unanswered user question (NonIntegerSRC issue 4), with no timings, CPU, compiler or flags and an unnamed 'Sinc' comparator; the harness it refers to (NonIntegerSRC src/src_test.cpp) times an older vendored mono Surge copy (src/src_utils/LanczosResampler.h), not the sst-basic-blocks header, and its CMakeLists.txt sets no build type or optimization flags. No number with a stated setup is reachable, so D.

corrections.caveats: Only evidence is an unanswered user question in another repository (jatinchowdhury18/NonIntegerSRC issue 4, opened 2026-05-18, no replies): 'the Lanczos interpolation was faster by a factor of two on my machine', with no CPU, compiler, flags, timings or library versions, and the issue does not say whether the 'Sinc' comparator was libsamplerate (SRC_SINC_FASTEST, the harness's sinc option) or the Holters-Parker resampler. The harness (src/src_test.cpp) wall-clocks one pass over a 1,000,000-sample sine per conversion with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock, one run, no warm-up. It times NonIntegerSRC's vendored 2021 Surge LanczosResampler (src/src_utils/LanczosResampler.h, mono, SSE intrinsics), not sst-basic-blocks' current header (include/sst/basic-blocks/dsp/LanczosResampler.h, templated on block size, stereo, SIMD via sst simd-ops); the libsamplerate wrapper (src/LibSamplerRateSRC.h) runs one channel. CMakeLists.txt sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE or optimization flags and the README builds with plain 'cmake -Bbuild', so a single-config Linux build may be unoptimized. The work differs in quality: the Lanczos kernel is A=4 (8 taps, table-interpolated), far shorter than libsamplerate's band-limited sinc filters, so a 2x speed gap at lower filter quality is not a like-for-like win. The NonIntegerSRC README's own chart reports its Holters-Parker resampler 17-40x faster than libsamplerate, far above the Lanczos 2x. No libsamplerate or r8brain comparison and no benchmark exist in sst-basic-blocks itself. A snippet 'Lanczos 4.5x slower than sinc_best, 2x faster than sinc_fastest' traces to obspy issue 1213 (2015) about ObsPy's own Lanczos against scikits.samplerate, unrelated to Surge, and is not used. License: LanczosResampler.h is dual GPL-3.0/MIT per its header and README, but it includes sst/basic-blocks/simd/setup.h and mechanics/simd-ops.h, which are GPL-3.0-or-later only, so MIT reuse needs those includes and the sum_ps_to_float call replaced (the header says as much).

corrections.caveats: No benchmark against a named competitor on any reachable page. The wiki Home chart 'VVdeC Decoder Performance Over Time' (img/version_history_240205.png, read directly; values approximate) plots only VVdeC releases v0.1 to v2.2: about 299 fps RA ClassB, about 300 fps LBP ClassB, about 131 fps AI ClassB, about 79 fps RA ClassA and about 44 fps AI ClassA at v2.2, on VTM-10.0 encoded JVET CTC sequences, Xeon W-2155 @ 3.3 GHz, 20 threads; no compiler, flags or OS details beyond 'Linux'. The wiki 'Integration in FFmpeg' page says only 'As VVdeC is still faster and realtime capable'; gianni-rosato/mpv-build-vvc README says FFmpeg's native ffvvc 'is not nearly as performant as Fraunhofer's vvdec', also without numbers. The ffvvc/FFmpeg wiki gives FFVVC's own fps on i7-12700K, M1 and i7-11700K, which cannot be set against VVdeC's Xeon W-2155 chart. Snippet only, not opened (archive.fosdem.org and hhi.fraunhofer.de are EGRESS_BLOCKED): the FOSDEM 2024 handout by the FFVVC author reportedly says FFVVC C code is on par with VVdeC (VVdeC about 10 percent faster on Linux, about 10 percent slower on Windows) and that VVdeC with asm was about 90 percent faster single-threaded and 75 percent faster multi-threaded; that predates FFmpeg's x86 AVX2 VVC assembly, so the gap may have narrowed. OpenVVC paper (arXiv 2205.12217) claims are snippet only. Papers listed on the wiki Publications page (ICIP 2020, ACM MM'21, MHV '22/'23) are on blocked hosts. A retier from an environment that reaches archive.fosdem.org or arXiv could lift this to B.

corrections.caveats: Tier D because the repository has no speed numbers against LAME. Folklore only, not opened: Hydrogenaudio wiki and forum snippets (hydrogenaudio.org is blocked here) say Helix is roughly three times as fast as LAME, with figures such as x35 realtime versus x8 for LAME and a 5 minute song in 3.6 s with Helix versus 6.5 s with Xing; these are old posts of unknown settings and versions and were not measured on the hmp3 code. The fork L4cache/hmp3 (release 5.2.4 page) times only hmp3 builds against each other: an 85 min 03 s (5103 s) 48 kHz stereo PCM file on a Ryzen 7900X with gcc 14.1.0 and clang 18.1.6, 7.43 s (686.81x realtime) for the standard gcc build and 5.92 s (861.99x) for gcc-znver4-fast-math-pgo; no LAME run, and its encoder settings are not shown. License: the encoder in hmp3/ is under RPSL-1.0 (RealNetworks Public Source License 1.0, OSI-approved but reciprocal, with source-release duties on external deployment, and not GPL-compatible), with the RCSL as an alternative for RealNetworks licensees; files outside hmp3/ are MIT per the README and the Makefile header, and there is no root LICENSE file. The encoder is mixed C and C++ (bitallo*.cpp, mp3enc.cpp, srcc*.cpp, test/tomp3.cpp). MP3 patents have expired. Project is small (38 stars, 54 commits).
